titel: Active Listening, Reflecting Feelings, and Questioning

schritte.text:
Listening seems self-evident – and yet it is one of the most demanding counseling competencies. In everyday life, we often listen only until a story of our own, a piece of advice, or a judgment occurs to us. **Active listening**, a term that goes back to Rogers and was popularized by Thomas Gordon, among others, means by contrast **undivided, understanding listening** that is also reflected back to the other person.

Active listening comprises several levels:

- **Nonverbal attending:** an open, attentive posture, appropriate eye contact, a calm pace, nodding
- **Encouraging signals:** brief sounds or words such as “mm-hmm,” “yes,” “I see” that invite the person to continue speaking
- **Reflecting back what has been understood:** through paraphrasing (content) and reflecting feelings (emotions)
- **Asking when things are unclear:** “Have I understood you correctly that …?”
- **Tolerating pauses:** silence gives room for thinking and sensing

It is just as important to know what **hinders** active listening. Thomas Gordon described typical roadblocks to communication, such as ordering, warning, moralizing, premature advice-giving, criticizing, interpreting, reassuring, and diverting. They are often well meant but signal: “I know better than you what is good for you.”

Active listening has several **effects**: clients feel understood, put their thoughts in order while speaking, come into contact with their own feelings – and the counselor continuously checks their understanding.

schritte.frage: Is this active listening or a communication roadblock?

elemente.text: “Have I understood you correctly that it’s mainly the evenings that are hard?”
“If I were you, I’d quit immediately.”
(Remains silent for a few seconds, stays attentive, and gives the client time.)
“But you don’t say something like that about your own mother.”

schritte.erklaerung: Encouraging signals, clarifying questions, and attentive silence promote the conversation. Reassuring, advising, interpreting, and moralizing are among Gordon’s roadblocks to communication: they lead away from the person’s experience.

schritte.text:
In **paraphrasing**, the counselor restates the **factual core** of a statement **in their own words**. They summarize what they have understood without judging, interpreting, or adding anything.

Example:

- Client: “My boss keeps giving me new tasks, but the old ones aren’t finished yet. And then he’s surprised that nothing gets done on time.”
- Paraphrase: “You keep getting new tasks before the old ones are done – and in the end, the delays are blamed on you.”

Good paraphrasing is:

- **brief** – shorter than the original statement
- **in one’s own words** – not mere parroting, which quickly seems mechanical
- **tentative** – formulated as an offer that may be corrected (“If I understand you correctly …”)
- **focused on the essentials** – it selects what seems central

Paraphrases fulfill several functions: they **check** understanding, **structure** longer narratives, **slow down** the conversation, and give the client the opportunity to hear what has been said from the outside. After a paraphrase, clients often add something important of their own accord (“Yes, exactly – and actually the worst thing is that …”).

A special form is the **summary**, which bundles longer sections of the conversation. It is particularly suitable at transitions, for example before a change of topic or at the end of a session.

schritte.frage: A client says: “Since my mother-in-law moved in with us, I have no space for myself anymore. She interferes in everything – in parenting, in cooking, even in the laundry.” Which response is a successful paraphrase?
optionen: “Since your mother-in-law moved in with you, she has been interfering in many areas of your everyday life, and you hardly have any space for yourself anymore.”
“Your mother-in-law is obviously very domineering and controlling.”
“Have you ever talked to your husband about it?”
“Since my mother-in-law moved in with us, I have no space for myself anymore.”
schritte.erklaerung: The first response restates the core in one’s own words without judging. Option 2 interprets and judges the mother-in-law, option 3 is a question that shifts the topic, and option 4 repeats verbatim and therefore seems mechanical.

schritte.text:
Whereas paraphrasing reflects the content, **reflecting emotional content** (German: Verbalisieren emotionaler Erlebnisinhalte, VEE) is directed at the person’s **emotional experience**. The German term was coined primarily by Reinhard and Anne-Marie Tausch; in English one speaks of *reflection of feelings*.

The counselor names feelings, wishes, fears, and appraisals that **resonate** in the statement but are often not expressly stated.

Example:

- Client: “My boss keeps giving me new tasks, but the old ones aren’t finished yet. And then he’s surprised that nothing gets done on time.”
- Reflection of feeling: “That annoys you, and perhaps you also feel unfairly treated.”

Helpful pointers for reflecting feelings:

- **Name feelings as precisely as possible:** “disappointed,” “hurt,” “exhausted” are more precise than “bad.”
- **Match the intensity:** do not dramatize (“You are desperate”) when the person is slightly unsettled – and do not play it down when they are deeply shaken.
- **Formulate tentatively:** “It seems to me …,” “Could it be that …?” – the person is the expert on their own experience.
- **Stay close to the experience:** reflecting feelings is not interpretation (“That has to do with your father”) but putting into words what is present right now.
- **Pick up on ambivalence:** “On the one hand you are relieved; on the other hand you are also sad.”

Reflecting feelings deepens self-exploration and is regarded as the centerpiece of empathic understanding. It requires attentive perception of nonverbal signals as well: tone of voice, pauses, facial expression, posture.

schritte.frage: Is this a paraphrase or a reflection of emotional content?

elemente.text: “You have postponed the exam twice, and now the last date is coming up.”
“There’s a lot of pressure – and perhaps also the fear of not making it again.”
“Your son moved out three months ago and has rarely been in touch since.”
“It sounds as if you miss him very much – and as if it hurts that he gets in touch so rarely.”
“Since the spring, you have been working in two teams at the same time.”
“You seem relieved when you talk about it.”

schritte.erklaerung: Paraphrases restate facts and circumstances; reflections of feeling name feelings, wishes, and fears. In practice, the two are often combined, for example: “You work in two teams – and that is increasingly exhausting you.”

schritte.text:
Questions direct attention – and thus the conversation. The distinction between open and closed questions is fundamental.

**Open questions** cannot be answered with a single word. They often begin with **wh-words** such as “how,” “what,” “when,” “where,” or with invitations such as “Tell me …”. They invite exploration and leave it to the client to decide what they consider important.

- “How are you getting on with the new situation?”
- “What brought you to us today?”

**Closed questions** can be answered with yes/no or a brief piece of information. They are useful for **clarifying facts**, bringing about **decisions**, or making targeted assessments in **crises**.

- “How old are your children?”
- “Have you ever thought about taking your own life?”

Questions become problematic in the following forms:

- **Question cascades:** several questions in a row are overwhelming (“How was that, and what did you do then, and did your husband say anything?”).
- **Leading questions:** they suggest the answer (“Surely you also think that …?”).
- **Why-questions:** they can be experienced as pressure to justify oneself (“Why did you do that?”). Rephrasing often helps: “What prompted you to do that?” or “How did that come about?”.
- **Interrogation character:** a sequence of many closed questions makes the person passive.

A rule of thumb from motivational interviewing is: **more reflections than questions**. Anyone who first reflects what they have heard after a question deepens the conversation and avoids a question-and-answer game.

schritte.frage: Which of the following questions are open questions? (Multiple answers possible)
optionen: “What would you like from our conversation?”
“How do you experience the situation at home?”
“Tell me what a typical day looks like for you.”
schritte.erklaerung: Open questions and invitations to tell invite more detailed answers. “Have you …?” and “Are you …?” are closed questions that are usually answered with yes or no. Both kinds of questions have their place – what matters is using them deliberately.

schritte.text: The question “Why did you cancel the appointment?” can be experienced as {{pressure to justify oneself|appreciation|a paraphrase}}. A more helpful formulation would be: “{{How did it come about that you canceled the appointment?|You surely didn’t have a reason, did you?|Why exactly was that?}}”
schritte.erklaerung: Why-questions easily sound like a reproach. A “how did it come about” question invites the person to tell their story without demanding justification. The other two options are leading or remain within the why-structure.

schritte.einleitung: Constructed situation: You work in the human resources department. Mr. D., 52, a long-standing employee, comes to you after a restructuring.

runden.klient: “I’ve been working here for 25 years, and all of a sudden I’m supposed to answer to a 30-year-old team leader who explains to me how to do my job.”

antworten.text: “That’s just how it is these days; the young ones bring a breath of fresh air.”
antworten.feedback: The response relativizes and judges. Mr. D. is unlikely to feel either heard or taken seriously.

antworten.text: “Why didn’t you apply for the position yourself?”
antworten.feedback: A why-question at this point comes across as a reproach and distracts from his experience.

antworten.text: “After 25 years of experience, it evidently feels hurtful to receive instructions from someone considerably younger.”
antworten.feedback: Paraphrasing and reflecting feelings are combined: the factual core (25 years, younger supervisor) and the possible feeling (hurt) are reflected back.

runden.klient: “Hurtful, yes. As if everything I’ve built up here were worth nothing.”

antworten.text: “You’re worried that your achievements and your experience are no longer seen.”
antworten.feedback: The reflection picks up on the deeper fear – lack of recognition – and deepens understanding.

antworten.text: “That’s not true – of course it’s worth something!”
antworten.feedback: The contradiction is well meant but passes over his experience. Mr. D. now tends to have to defend himself.

antworten.text: “How many employees did you train in the past, and in which departments?”
antworten.feedback: Factual questions are premature here and distract from the emotional core.

runden.klient: “Exactly. And to be honest, I don’t even know whether I want to hold out like this until retirement.”

antworten.text: “Then you should think about partial retirement.”
antworten.feedback: Premature advice skips over clarification. Mr. D. has not yet said what he wants.

antworten.text: “A fundamental question has come up for you right now. What would be important to you so that you could enjoy working here again?”
antworten.feedback: The response reflects the significance of the issue and, with an open question, opens up space for his own wishes and values.

antworten.text: “Lots of people say that, but in the end everyone stays.”
antworten.feedback: The generalization devalues his statement and closes down the conversation.

schritte.text: Paraphrasing reflects what was said; reflecting feelings reflects what is experienced in saying it. Open questions open up space, closed questions clarify facts – and reflecting more than asking keeps the conversation with the client.

schritte.frage: Which of Gordon’s communication roadblocks do you yourself use most often when you are under time pressure?
schritte.hinweis: Over the next few days, pay conscious attention to your spontaneous reactions in conversations. How often do you give advice, reassure, or divert? How could you paraphrase or reflect feelings instead?
